intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that multiple epiphyseal dysplasia-2 (EDM2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding the alpha-2 chain of type IX collagen (COL9A2) on chromosome 1p32.3-p33.

paragraphs.text: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED) is a dominantly inherited chondrodysplasia characterized by mild short stature and early-onset osteoarthrosis (Briggs et al., 1994). The EDM2 form is a subtype of MED in which the hips are not markedly affected at an early age. From childhood, patients have pain and stiffness of the knees, ankles, elbows, and finger joints, and they are prone to early degenerative joint disease (Fiedler et al., 2002).

paragraphs.text: Barrie et al. (1958) published a report titled 'Multiple epiphysial dysplasia.'

Versteylen et al. (1988) described 2 families that appeared to have multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. Severe osteochondritis of the knees was strikingly common in both families. The authors suggested that the osteochondritis was caused by the fragmented and maldeveloped epiphyses typical of epiphyseal dysplasia.

paragraphs.text: Fiedler et al. (2002) reported a family of 19 individuals over 4 generations, of whom 12 had a variant of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia with relative sparing of the hips during childhood. Beginning in childhood, the disease caused pain and stiffness of the knees, ankles, elbows, and finger joints. Some adult patients had repeated episodes of free articular bodies that caused locking of the joint. Affected individuals were prone to early degenerative joint disease. On electron microscopy, the diameter of collagen fibrils from free articular bodies removed arthroscopically from 2 patients did not differ obviously from that of normal articular cartilage.

paragraphs.text: Briggs et al. (1994) performed linkage studies in a large family with MED. Linkage to the chromosome 19 interval previously linked to pseudoachondroplasia and a form of MED was excluded. Using this family, the authors identified an MED locus, designated EDM2, on the short arm of chromosome 1. This region contains the COL9A2 gene, which encodes the alpha-2 chain of type IX collagen, a structural component of the cartilage extracellular matrix.

paragraphs.text: In a 4-generation family with EDM2, Fiedler et al. (2002) screened candidate regions and identified a G-to-C substitution at position -1 in the exon 3/intron 3 splicing region of the COL9A2 gene. The authors considered it most likely that this change alters splicing. They confirmed the substitution in 8 clinically affected family members and in 3 presymptomatic young children, using both automated sequencing and BsaWI digestion of amplicons. Fiedler et al. (2002) concluded that, together with previous reports, their results indicated that mutations causing skipping of exon 3 within the COL3 domain of the alpha-2 chain of collagen IX may be relatively common in patients with the MED subtype in which the hips are not markedly affected at an early age.
